body.heading: Same sound, different word
paragraphs: Homophones are words that are pronounced identically but differ in meaning and usually in spelling. Sea and see, right and write, pair and pear, their, there and they're — English is full of these sound twins, which is why spelling tests and autocorrect both have such a hard life.
Some sets are generous: to, too and two; buy, by and bye; and the champion trio of right, write and rite, with wright (a maker, as in playwright) making four for the very keen.

body.heading: Why they exist
paragraphs: English borrowed words from many languages and then let pronunciation drift for a thousand years. Knight once had its k and gh sounded out loud; as speech softened, words that once sounded different collapsed into the same shape, leaving spelling to remember the difference.
That history makes homophones a gift for jokes. “Why did the baker stop making doughnuts? He got tired of the hole thing” only works because whole and hole share a sound.

body.heading: Try it: the homophone sentence game
paragraphs: Take turns building the silliest correct sentence you can using a homophone pair: “The knight spent the night guarding the castle.” Score a point for each pair used correctly, and two points if the sentence makes somebody laugh.
For a drawing version, one player draws a homophone — a flower made of flour, perhaps — and everyone else guesses which spelling was meant. The arguments about the answer are the best part.

takeaway: Homophones prove that English spelling remembers things English speech has forgotten — and they are endless fun to play with.
